Mr. Money Mustache September 5, 2023, 2:56 pm

I’m usually in favor of at least 20%, because when you work out the effective interest rate increase that PMI is hitting you with, it usually works out to a very good return on that extra 10%.

For example, imagine a 500k house, and you are debating between a 50k or 100k downpayment (10 or 20%). And let’s say the interest rate is down at 5%.

If the PMI premium is a typical 0.8% of the loan value $450k, you’d be paying an extra $3600 per year in PMI premiums. Just for the privilege of not putting down the extra $50k.

That’s 7% of the potential extra downpayment that gets eaten up every year!

Or to put it another way, if you put in the second $50k, you are earning 5% in foregone loan interest PLUS 7% in saved PMI premiums. 12% in total, which is the best return around.

It’s a similar return when deciding between a 15 vs 30 year mortgage (the 15 year mortgage provides the extra risk free return). The return decreases the longer one keeps the mortgage, but for most people who move / re-finance within 7 years or so, it’s well worth it.

My brother got a mortgage from Navy Federal Credit Union with no PMI. So those deals are out there. This is not a VA loan, just standard mortgage. I’m thinking other credit unions might offer the same.

My mortgage is 2.5% – P&I is $886/mo. Last year, we had about 28 years left and the interest was slightly higher than the principal payment each month – about $450/mo. or so in interest. Did a lump sum payment and cut off about 15 years of payments – now almost all my payment goes to the principal. The interest each month is now only about $230/mo.

In this sense, the savings in interest each month is about equal to what I’d be earning if I’d kept the lump sum in a money market. I’ve also got peace of mind because A. if I didn’t make another extra payment, I’ll still have a paid-for house in about 13 years, and B. since the money is already spent on the mortgage, it removes the temptation to find something else to use it on.

So the short answer to your comment is: yes, the front-loaded nature of the mortgage does factor into the equation. From an interest savings perspective, it’s definitely more profitable to pay the mortgage down during the first half of the amortization versus the last half.

As I understand it, the front-loaded nature of interest on a mortgage is just a reflection (the mirror image, maybe) of compound interest. So an extra principal payment in year 1 of a 30 year fixed-rate mortgage has a greater impact than one in year 25 because it has longer to compound, not because it gives a greater rate of return.

If you make an extra payment of $100 this year, next year your balance will be lower by $102.85. And in 27 years your balance will be lower by $100*1.0285^27=$213.56.

But if instead you put $100 in your high-yield savings account, next year you will have $105. So you really will approach the payoff amount faster that way (as long as the interest rate you’re earning remains higher).

You understand it correctly! You don’t pay more or less interest as a percentage of your loan by paying it off early or by paying it for 30 years – when you make extra payments early, you simply borrowed the total amount of money for less time. Naturally you pay less aggregate interest if you pay the loan off early, because you borrowed the total sum for less time. If your mortgage is 5%, for example, the total interest you pay as a percentage of what you borrowed will be 5% regardless of whether you pay off the loan in year 1 or year 30. Amortized payments confuse people into thinking that they’re paying more interest in the beginning than the end – no, you’re paying the percentage of whatever is outstanding. The amortization just allows one to have the same payment over the life of the loan, rather than a huge payment now and a itty bitty payment later. So it appears that you are paying more in interest, but it’s just that the interest that is owed is a greater percentage of the payment amount in the beginning because you owe more money.

In any case, you are totally correct that in a static situation paying yourself $100 into a 5% bank account instead of paying $100 extra to a 2.75% mortgage will earn you the delta (5-2.75 =2.25%) real annual return, compounded. Of course there’s no guarantee the savings return remains at 5%, whereas the interest rate on the fixed mortgage is guaranteed to be 2.75%.

Just curious, what the logic is behind paying down a 2.75% mortgage when you can take the funds instead and place them in t-bills or cds and get 5-5.5% return? If a return greater than 2.75% was not an option I would understand. Paying off a mortgage is a great feeling but when interest returns are this high there are better options.

I am based in Germany and snagged a historically low interest rate of .87% on my mortgage. The difference is that it is fixed for 10 years so this business of prediction is indeed quite critical to my short and mid term financial planning.

I have had the mindset of paying off the place as rapidly as possible just as a bit of a hedge on the long term uncertainty of life. I figure, worst case scenario with a paid off home I can ride off into the sunset. However, I like my job and see myself in my field at least another 20 years (I am 33). Hence, I have a bit of a challenge as interest rate predictions would seem to drive my behavior greatly: Option 1 – pay off a super low return mortgage to hedge a long term increasing rate Option 2 – pay off the minimum on my mortgage and invest the remainder because the delta is so massive due to the historic rate I snagged Option 3 – some hybrid of the two

There’s the option of an accelerated pay-off of my mortgage every year so I have until December to decide as I save throughout the year, but it is always interesting times as I do find I need to develop an opinion on the whole mortgage situation.

Option 2 makes the most sense to me. If you want to be conservative you can always invest the additional funds in some type of interest bearing account — in the US that would be something like FDIC insured CDs currently at over 5%, not sure what the German equivalent might be. Then, after 10 years you can use everything saved in the conservative interest bearing accounts and apply it to the mortgage all at once. You’ll have benefitted from the difference in interest rates.

Yes, the delta is massive, so take advantage of it if you have the discipline to not spend the money elsewhere!

Interest rates are like the weather, easy conversation with anybody but nothing you can really effect. And if it happens to you, it’s usually not tragic. For most people, excessive focus on interest rates can be distracting from more important decisions / choices.

Most people aren’t $250k/yr+ software types. Most people are teachers, government workers, office workers and even factory workers. There are areas of the USA that are frightfully expensive to live in … housing, taxes, transportation and even the need for private education because of failing schools.

For most people the more important decision is where you live and work and not the interest rate on your mortgage. For example, teacher in San Jose CA might make 15%-20% more than a teacher in East Cobb GA. But a home in San Jose will be close to 4x the price of a home in East Cobb. If you aren’t competing with high comp careers, you will have a nicer home earlier in your career and it will cost way less each month. Not everyone wants or can move across the country, but more should consider it. Even lesser distance choices like Sacramento show the difference in lifestyle potential. That $400k home in East Cobb at 8% w/20% down is about $3k/mo (15yr). That SJ $1.4mil home would be over $8k/mo even if the interest rate was half (4%). And the difference in down payment is huge. And taxes and insurance aren’t even discussed here.

Life is easier and way less stressful if housing cost is zero. The path to zero is faster with lower cost housing in lower cost areas. I’ve seen many extended family members move from high cost NYC and NY State. All have better pay, better homes, better schools and way lower cost of living. Life changing for all of them.

For those who live on normal household incomes, where your home is might be way more important than any interest rate.

As far as investments go, if you are not an experienced financial professional or trader, interest rates are irrelevant. You can’t time interest rates or the market. The 80/20 rule (VTSAX/Bonds) rebalanced annually is the safest path for almost everyone. Anything else is really just a guess and sometimes a guess doesn’t work out well.

Housing costs will never be zero, because you still have to maintain the building. Survey every 8 years, new roof every 50 years, repointing every x years, new y every z years…

ChrisD: absolutely true. A bit of a rhetorical flourish on my part. But the carry cost of the physical structure is usually a modest 1% or 2% annually. You are better off with only this expense vs this plus mortgage.

But let’s not lose sight of the two key points.

1. A $400k home is easier to acquire, payoff and maintain then a similar home in a HCOL area that costs $1.4 million. Even with a much higher interest rate on the low priced home.

2. Once a home is owned “free and clear”, life is less stressful. More monthly cash to spend or save. Less likely to be tragically impacted by job interruption or negative financial event.

Where you choose to live has much more impact on your financial security than interest rates. Especially if you are a ‘normal’ person vs the huge income technology guy.

Keep in mind that a HCOL area is generally speaking more desirable than a LCOL area, otherwise it wouldn’t be so expensive. A highly paid software engineer in Silicon Valley could live in a much nicer house at a lower cost in a LCOL area even when factoring in the paycut, but for every person that leaves a drove of other people is ready to take their place.

MMM, you have been a keen supporter of including REITs in your portfolio. However there are particular challenges for REITs in a rising interest rate environment. Would you advocate holding any existing allocation to REITs or reduce the holdings. Is there an optimum allocation to REITs? I have a 10% allocation and feel uncomfortable with this.

If you’re in REITs, beware of anything involving commercial property right now, including bigger multifamily housing. Unlike regular residential loans, these always wind up financed with ARMs with shorter terms, like 5-year or 7-year. With the rising rates, any of these forced to refinance in the current climate are likely to default or be much less profitable if they do survive. Some are forecasting GFC level crashes, this time on the commercial side as opposed to residential (which should be just fine).

Look at the Return on Assets the REIT (or any company) generates. Is this greater than or less than the interest they’ll have to pay to refinance their debts?

If they are earning less on their assets than it costs to finance the assets, expect losses or dividend cuts as they deleverage. E.g. they are borrowing at 6% to hold assets yielding 3%.

Lots of REITs with negative cash flows are in an unsustainable position. It would make sense for them to start shedding assets that no longer earn their cost of capital instead of burning cash while hoping for rates to fall. But when everyone does that…

Another misconception unrelated to your comment that is worth noting is that if the Fed cuts rates that the 10yr and mortgages will come down.  They will come down some but that is related to the option adjusted spread on the mortgage (don’t worry about what that part means, that’s maybe a 0.5%-0.75% swing factor).  Mortgages price off of longer dated treasury rates (~10yr treasury or blend of 5 and 10yr) and these are already baking in a series of cuts beginning in 2024.  So the cuts would need to be more significant than people expect to move mortgage rates significantly.  In other words, if the Fed cuts short term rates in an orderly fashion to 3.5% mortgages might not move all (aside from that option adjusted spread) and the yield curve might just look normal again.

#8776. The Lat Training Guide For Building a Stronger and Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Most lifters want lats for one reason:  the V-taper. Well-developed lats give your upper body that powerful look from the front, side, and back, and yes, they make T-shirts fit better.

Besides looking awesome, the lats keep your shoulders stable, support better upper-body posture, and connect your arms to your torso, improving form during heavy lifts. Strong lats improve pulling mechanics, create a stronger pressing setup, and help your upper back stay in a better position during squats and deadlifts.

Here we’ll go over all things lats, including:

By the end, you’ll know how to train your lats for a stronger back, better pulls, healthier shoulders, and an upper body that will fill out your T-shirts.

The latissimus dorsi—or lats for short—are the body’s widest muscles and cover much of the back. They’re broad, flat, and fan-shaped, which is why well-developed lats help create that V-Taper look.

Because of their size, the lats attach to the

Because they attach to the upper arm and spine, they influence both shoulder movement and posture.

They also help with scapular depression, which pulls the shoulders down away from your ears and is an important part of good pulling form. Train those actions well, and you’ll build a wider back, stronger pulls, and better control from your shoulders through your hips.

We all know that lats are the engine behind rows, pull-ups, and chin-ups, but some don’t realize the vital role they play beyond them.

During the deadlift, strong, engaged lats help keep the bar close to your body as you pull. When the bar drifts away, the lift gets harder, and your lower back gets unhappy.

Your lats matter during the bench press, too. When engaged, they help create a stable base to press from, improve your pressing path, and transfer force from your leg drive to your upper body.

That is why strong lats aren’t just a “back day” thing: they set the table for better pressing form.

Pulling your lats down and back creates upper-body tightness for barbell back squat. Doing so helps stabilize the bar and keeps you in a stronger, more upright position instead of folding forward into a good morning.

The lats also matter for shoulder health and posture because they influence shoulder position and upper-body alignment. When the lats are balanced in length, they let the shoulder blades rest flat, and the shoulders open back naturally. This supports better posture.

And yes, they matter outside the gym, too. Pulling open heavy doors, climbing, carrying objects close to your body, and lifting things from the floor all involve the lats. Bigger lats create the look, but stronger lats help you pull, brace, carry, and move well.

Because the lats are large and their muscle fibers run in different directions, train them through several pulling paths. You need vertical pulling, horizontal pulling, straight-arm work, loaded stretches, and good form to keep the tension where it belongs.

You know the exercises, but that’s only part of it. For maximum growth and strength, keep these four things in mind.

Progressive Overload: Add load, reps, sets, range of motion, or better control over time. But don’t sacrifice lat tension, shoulder position, or form to move more weight.

Here are general recommendations that work for most lifters most of the time.

Use sets of three to six reps on heavier pulls. Good options include weighted pull-ups, heavy chin-ups, and lat pulldowns. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between sets, and keep the reps clean.

Use sets of eight to 15 reps on pulldowns, rows, dumbbell rows to the hip, seated machine rows, or cable rows. This is your bread-and-butter hypertrophy work. Use a full range of motion, control the stretch, and finish each rep by pulling the elbows toward the ribs or hips, depending on the exercise.

Use sets of 12 to 20 reps on straight-arm pulldowns, kneeling straight-arm pulldowns, cable pullovers, and band straight-arm pulldowns. These are great for lifters who struggle to feel their lats because these exercises isolate them.

Straight-arm pulldown variations are useful before deadlifting because engaging the lats helps maintain a neutral spine and keep the bar close. One or two sets of 10 to 15 reps work well as a primer.

Most lifters can train the lats directly two to three times per week.

Think of 12 to 16 direct lat sets per week as your weekly target. How you divide those sets depends on your goal.

If strength is the priority, spend more sets in the 3 to 6 rep range with weighted pull-ups, heavy pulldowns, chin-ups, and rows. If size is the goal, focus more work in the 8 to 15 rep range with pulldowns, rows, single-arm work, and machine or cable variations. If you struggle to feel your lats, include 12 to 20 rep sets of straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers, or band work.

Here’s an example of how to organize your weekly volume. 12 weekly sets might include four heavier sets, six muscle-building sets, and two higher-rep straight-arm sets. That gives you a fantastic combination of strength, size, and lat connection.

Using too much weight you cannot control might stroke the ego, but it does nothing for your gains. Here are a few more mistakes to watch out for to get the most out of your lat training.

Your hands hold the bar, but your elbows should lead the movement. When lifters focus only on pulling with their hands, chin-ups, pulldowns, and rows often turn into biceps-heavy exercises with a side order of forearm fatigue.

Fix: Drive your elbows down during pulldowns, pull your elbows toward your hips during rows, and tuck your shoulder blades into your back pocket for chin-ups.

Many lifters cut the top of pulldowns, pull-ups, and straight-arm exercises short. That leaves a lot of potential lat tension on the table, because the lats love a loaded stretch.

Fix: Reach overhead or forward under control, keep the ribs down, and feel the stretch without dumping on the shoulder joint. The goal is to control a stretch, not just hang through the connective tissue.

When the ribs flare, the lower back often arches, turning a lat exercise into a lower-back exercise. This can happen during pulldowns, pullovers, and straight-arm work when someone tries to create range they don’t own.

Fix: Keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis by breathing out and bracing the core on top of that. This gives the lats a better chance to lengthen and shorten without the lower back taking over.

If your shoulders shrug toward your ears during rows or pulldowns, your upper traps dominate. Doing so takes the focus off the lats and can lead to upper trap and neck pain.

Fix: Remember to keep your shoulders away from your ears and your chest up. You do this by keeping your neck long.

Lat training has its share of gym myths because everyone wants a wider back. Some advice sounds good until you realize it ignores range of motion, elbow path, body position, and the fact that your biceps will love to steal the show if you let them.

Wide-grip pulldowns and pull-ups are great, but they aren’t magic—and they don’t build wide lats. A wide grip doesn’t automatically increase lat tension. In fact, it often shortens your range of motion, limits the load, and shifts stress to the shoulders and upper back for many lifters. Shoulder-width, medium, and neutral grips offer a longer ROM, and you can lift more weight.

Pull-ups and chin-ups are gold-standard lat builders—but the lats need more. The problem is that pull-ups lock you into a single line of pull. Because the lats are large and wide, with muscle fibers running in different directions, dumbbell and machine variations let you adjust your body position and grips to change the line of pull and target muscle fibers that chin-ups miss.

Rows hammer the upper back, but they can also hit the lats with the right setup, grip, and elbow path. Rowing high with flared elbows shifts more attention to the traps, rear delts, and upper back. Rowing back toward the hip with your elbow close gives the lats more work.

They assist with deadlifts, squats, bench press setup, posture, and shoulder control. So yes, train them for width. But don’t forget they also help you lift better when no one is admiring your V-taper.

The lats don’t need a separate “back day or bust” approach. You can train them hard during an upper-body session or weave them into a full-body workout.

Goal: Build lat size and strength while still training the chest, shoulders, upper back, and arms.

Goal: Train the lats as part of a full-body workout.

The winning formula is this: Train the lats with vertical pulls, rows, straight-arm work, single-arm variations, and exercises that challenge the stretch position. Keep the ribs down, control the shoulders, pull toward the hips to engage more lats, and stop letting your biceps, traps, and lower back take over.

Remember to lock the lats in during your squat, bench, and deadlift because they are the difference between a sloppy rep and a clean one. Use enough volume to grow and enough weight to build muscle and strength, but never shortchange the range of motion.

If you do it right, you’ll need to buy larger shirts.

#8770. Weini Kelati Has Taken a One-Mile at a Time Approach for Taking On the NYC Marathon

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There was a time when eight miles felt like an eternity to Weini Kelati. Now, toward the tail end of preparing for her first full marathon, she can find herself 10 miles into a 20-mile workout and realize the distance that once signaled the end of a hard day has now become the halfway point.

This progression says a lot about what marathon preparation requires. The obvious difference between a half marathon and 26.2 miles is distance, but Kelati discovered that building a marathon body involved more than adding more miles to her workload. The body must be conditioned to tolerate additional volume, know how to fuel, how to recover, and eventually trust that the work was enough when fatigue arrives.

Kelati, the American half-marathon record holder, Olympian, and five-time national champion will make her marathon debut at the TCS New York City Marathon on Nov. 1. Speaking with Muscle & Fitness through New York Road Runners, she explained that she had always seen the half marathon as a gateway toward eventually racing 26.2, even giving herself a loose requirement of completing four or five before considering making the move.

“I think first I was nervous,” Kelati said. “I was like, ‘Oh my goodness. This is going to be hard because I used to be at low mileage.’”

What surprised her most isn’t how difficult the transition was, but how quickly the human body can begin adjusting to something once intimidating as simply another day in training.

During Kelati’s half-marathon preparation, she said her highest weekly mileage reached around 75 miles. For this build, she knew that number would have to climb into the 90s. The increase initially made her nervous. Once she started, however, something unexpected happened: She began enjoying it.

The biggest adjustment was redefining what constitutes a long effort. In the lead-up to a 10K or half-marathon, a six- or eight-mile tempo run could represent one of the bigger sustained sessions on her schedule. Marathon preparation introduced two different types of long runs, including easier road efforts and workouts, which she can cover approximately 20 miles at a specific pace.

“I’m not the type of person who rushes into something,” Kelati said. “I always take a lot baby steps to get used to something.”

That patience allowed her body to establish a new baseline without making every unfamiliar distance feel like a test. Her weekly structure wasn’t radically different from half-marathon training, either. The biggest change is that familiar paces and workouts extended further, asking her to sustain what she already knew for considerably longer.

The result was a changed internal relationship with distance.

“When you get to eight miles, you start saying, ‘Oh, I’m already halfway,’ instead of saying, ‘Oh, I used to stop here,” Kelati says. “The mind and the body change the way I have to handle it.”

The added mileage exposed an area Kelati admits hasn’t always been a strength for her: nutrition.

At shorter distances, she could get away with habits that weren’t conducive with marathon preparation. For years, she could wake up and run without eating anything because consuming food before a morning session wasn’t something she enjoyed.

The marathon build forced her to adjust that part of her routine. When there is a large increase in workload, personal preferences eventually run into physical necessity.

“You have to help the body as much as it’s working,” Kelati said. “During the marathon training, you have to fuel your body. You have to get ready for the next hard run.”

She learned that fueling for her bigger sessions didn’t mean forcing down a huge meal. If appetite was an issue, she would have smaller meals spaced throughout the day. This same logic changed her behavior after a run.

Meals were the common recovery method for Kelati,  but the increased workload led her to incorporate recovery drinks and pay closer attention to getting nutrition back into her body sooner.

Kelati’s favorite recovery method didn’t require scheduling or involve any expensive equipment.

“I love taking naps after every single run,” she said. “It doesn’t matter how hard or easy the run I do, I just have to take a little nap every day and, of course, more than eight hours of sleep during the night.”

Kelati fully believes giving her body adequate downtime has been an important reason she was able to absorb demanding training and be able to show up the following morning and ask her body to perform again.

There is one part of marathon preparation Kelati couldn’t completely simulate.

She could run 20 miles in training, nap after training, and ask experienced marathoners what waits beyond the distances she already knows.

Until New York, however, she won’t know exactly how her own body and mind will respond to racing 26.2 miles. That uncertainty doesn’t seem to bother her as much as thinking about the entire distance at once.

“I don’t like counting the miles,” Kelati said. “It seems pretty long for me to think about it while you’re standing on the start line or you just started. You’re in the first mile, and you’re just like, ‘Oh, we have like 25 miles to go.’”

Instead, she intends on remaining completely in the moment.

“I just like to be in the present and focus one mile at a time,” she said.

Insights have helped. Kelati did the same thing before moving into half marathons, quizzing runners about which points of the race are the most challenging so she could have some idea of what awaited her. This time, the answer is a different number.

“They keep saying, ‘You’re going to start racing when you get to 30K,’” she says. “It can be different, but also it’ll give you what to expect or what’s coming when you get to that distance and how you’re going to handle it.”

Discomfort will eventually arrive, and Kelati’s strategy is a simple one. She reminds herself that the pain is temporary and that she’d rather find out what she’s capable of than finish wondering whether she would have given more.

It’s a mindset that comes from weeks of watching her body handle workloads she once was uncertain about. Kelati says one of the things she’s most proud of during this build has been how naturally she adapted to the training her coach put in front of her. Each completed run and training session has chipped away the stone of uncertainty that existed when 26.2 was still just a thought.

“When you try to do something new, you always have these thoughts that can prevent you from doing something,” Kelati said. “But then once you just start doing it, I feel like we can do anything when we believe.”

When Kelati reaches the start line in Staten Island, there will be lots of thoughts in her head. All the early morning runs, how well she’s done in races in New York, and all the months spent gradually extending what her body can tolerate.

She will let those thoughts flow. Her goal for that morning speaks to her readiness.

“I want to feel good just standing there and say, ‘Today is a great day,’” Kelati said. ‘“I feel good. Let’s do this.’”

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. #8756. JASON AVELAR AND GARRETT BEAL SHARE THE STORY OF PRESCOTT JUNIOR HIGH’S LEGACY OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION EXCELLENCE

President Donald Trump announced the re-establishment and restoration of the Presidential Fitness Test on July 31, 2025, when he signed an Executive Order revitalizing the test along with the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition. Since then, the Trump administration also announced the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, a competition which invites “schools, districts, and youth-serving organizations to design and execute creative, repeatable models that inspire student participation, teamwork, and enthusiasm for the Presidential Fitness Test (PFT).”

One school that could serve as an example for others to follow and may be a top contender should they enter that challenge would be Prescott Junior High School in Modesto, California. The school overall has a great reputation, but it is best known for their P.E. program. Current teachers Jason Avelar and Garrett Beal are two of the teachers for this program, but its legacy as a fitness-focused juggernaut goes back nearly a half-century.

Beal, who also served as a police officer for a period of his life, played sports as a kid but credited a high school wrestling coach for introducing him to the weight room.

“It was the first sport where I saw that being strong helped,” he said. “I fell in love even more with fitness than wrestling.”

Avelar was bitten by the iron bug while playing football in his high school days but also found he had natural leadership skills as a linebacker. His coaches confirmed this and could have played a role in him becoming a gym teacher.

“I had a few coaches and teachers pull me aside and said, ‘Hey, I think you’d be a great teacher.’”

Both Beal and Alevar are reminded often about the history they are a part of. Modeled closely after the La Sierra High School Physical Education Program (the famous 1960s President’s Council on Physical Fitness model) Prescott’s program has challenged junior high students for decades using a high-standard and military-inspired structure.

In 1973, then Prescott P.E. teacher Mark Wilson saw a demonstration of a high-intensity, physical fitness-based curriculum. Wilson was inspired by the concept and used his own version on his students, challenging them to make fitness a priority at an early age.

There is a color and points based system to help gauge the students’ progress and motivate them to work harder. All students start with zero points and white trunks, and there are 20 different fitness tests. Each test offers one, two, or four points for their performances. Once a student achieves 60 points, they earn red trunks. However, the scoring goes back to zero because they are at a new level with harder challenges. Once they work back up to 60 points, they then earn blue trunks.

“The tests at that point get very challenging,” Avelar said. There are also gold and purple trunks for those students that do very well in the program. Prescott even has a P.E. Hall of Fame, where students can be recognized. Avelar acknowledged one student who even cleared the purple trunk scoring early, meaning they had to create a new level just for her.

“We decided on custom trunks. Once you pass purple, you get to pick your own.”

The bars may be seen as super high for some, but Avelar and Beal share that either students rise to the occasion and reach it, or they get closer than they may have had there not been that high bar in the first place.

The results speak for themselves. One student ran two miles in 12 minutes, 27 seconds. Another performed over 6,000 continuous sit-ups, and multiple students have reportedly performed over 1,000 unbroken pushups. The Prescott program has had a generational impact in Modesto.

Beal said, “I wear my Prescott shirt anywhere around town, and people stop to talk to me about when they went there.” He even met one man at a book club, and he recognized the last name on their Hall of Fame wall.

Other teachers at Prescott were also students there, and both Beal and Avelar confirmed that they strive to be the best examples possible by making their wellness a priority. They also said that even though the high school P.E. programs may not have as intense of programs, the students who went to Prescott continue their fitness journeys after they move on. Others may take the school for granted but realize what they were a part of later on.

Avelar said, “As they leave, they realize ‘Oh crap, this is a super special place.’”

Both teachers take great pride in not only what they are a part of but having added their own chapters to the Prescott story. They are reminded of how important their work is every day, and they definitely don’t take the positions they are in for granted.

Avelar stated. “The fulfillment I get from showing up to school every day and seeing kids reach their goals, push themselves, do things they’ve never done before, and seeing the excitement on their faces is why I do it.”

Beal added, “This is such a special place to be,”

There is no official word on how many schools will enter the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, but both Avelar and Beal were pleased that the Presidential Fitness Test has been reinstated, and they hope that it can serve as a catalyst for other P.E. programs to do more to help their students embrace fitness, pushing themselves, and taking on great challenges. As they have seen first hand, the impact goes beyond the school walls and can last for many years to come.

To learn more about the PFT or the School Innovation Challenge, go to fitness.gov.

You can follow the Prescott program on Instagram @prescott_standard and Beal and Alevar on LinkedIn.

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

#8750. World Anti-Doping Agency’s Latest Banned List Sends a Warning to Athletes Looking for ‘Loopholes’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There is a certain kind of athlete who treats the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list like a treasure map. He reads it, finds something that isn’t printed there, and figures he’s discovered a loophole. The molecule has a name that sounds like a Wi-Fi password, the vial says “research use only,” and some guy with a podcast swears it repairs tendons, melts fat, or turns you into a gazelle. Perfect. What could possibly go wrong?

Well, WADA just made that little game harder. Its 2027 Prohibited List, which takes effect Jan. 1, now explicitly mentions peptides in the category for non-approved substances. The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency put out an advisory explaining the change and warning athletes not to assume an experimental peptide is legal simply because its particular alphabet soup isn’t spelled out on the list. That’s a useful distinction, because the peptide business has become a sprawling mess of legitimate medicine, promising research, questionable claims, and little bottles of who-the-hell-knows-what.

Before anybody starts screaming that WADA banned every peptide on earth, it didn’t. Peptides are chains of amino acids, and some are established medicines. Insulin is a peptide. The relevant category, called S0, covers pharmacological substances without approval for human therapeutic use by a government health authority anywhere in the world, provided they aren’t already covered by another prohibited class. Some peptides fall into other categories. The word “peptides” appearing in S0 is a clarification, not a declaration that every peptide drug is forbidden.

The important point is that experimental substances weren’t necessarily fair game yesterday. BPC-157, for example, was already prohibited under the rules for non-approved substances. Others, including certain growth-hormone-related compounds, are covered elsewhere. What changed is the language, making it even harder to pretend that an unlisted research chemical gets a free pass. And if you compete in a tested sport, “I couldn’t find it on Google” ranks right up there with road rage. No one is gonna buy it.

There are some other interesting additions as well. WADA names two experimental metabolic modulators, SLU-PP-332 and SLU-PP-915, as examples in its hormone and metabolic modulators category. The list also adds examples of diuretics and masking agents, including eplerenone and finerenone, drugs that have perfectly legitimate medical uses. That’s another reality athletes forget: the prohibited list isn’t just a catalog of things somebody invented to cheat. It can include ordinary prescription medications, depending on the drug and circumstances.

Meanwhile, semaglutide and tirzepatide, the active ingredients in two widely used families of weight-loss and diabetes treatments, remain on WADA’s monitoring program for 2027. Monitoring is not banning. WADA is collecting information about their use in sport; it has not put them on the prohibited list. The same distinction matters with caffeine, which is monitored in competition but not prohibited. Which makes me feel good that the people making the rules recognize a difference between watching something and convicting it.

While they were at it, they also tuned up the cannabis language. WADA clarified that psychoactive THC-related cannabinoids, including certain synthetic and semi-synthetic versions, are prohibited in competition. CBD itself isn’t prohibited, but a CBD product containing undeclared THC can still create a problem. Meaning, you run the risk of failing a drug test.

It doesn’t matter if you’re an Olympian, a fighter, a weightlifter, or some local competitor. Under anti-doping rules, athletes are responsible for what’s in their bodies. What’s missing off a label is not an alibi. Neither is a coach or a doctor. You’re on your own. So play the game wisely.

I am 100% for researching new performance drugs. That’s how some useful things eventually get discovered. But research is not approval, and a promising animal study is not proof in humans. None of that really matters to many athletes because they usually rely on anecdotal evidence. They will do it anyway—if they think it works and can find a way of not getting caught. Which, for the most part, in my view of things, they do. But if your competitive career matters to you, you need to be very careful, as peptides create a very broad gray area. Make sure you check the actual status of the substance before you put it in your body—and remember, just because WADA has banned it doesn’t mean that there’s a test for it. January isn’t far away, and WADA is making one thing abundantly clear: They’re always a step behind. I guess it never occurs to them to switch hats and discover the new stuff before we do.

#8744. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

As it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

I don’t know the details of culdesac, but much of what you say is fair in general. Our development system is quite broken as it depends on risk-adverse, profit-seeking developers to build out a communities’ land use vision, which may or may not be supportive of car-lite living in itself. It has resulted in sprawl and “luxury” everything sameness and widespread auto dependence. I agree ideally there would be lots of employment in the development, but I would argue that dense, transit accessible housing is the greater need in our system. Less regulation is often the answer here (e.g., removing parking minimums, increasing residential zoning density), but in your example, clearly some way of ensuring that the development follows through on its promises it made for approval is needed. On the flip side, any housing built, even if it is for AirBnbs is creating housing and likely converting other short term to long term rentals due to competition. Any dense housing in an area that isn’t car dependent is a win in my book, and culdesac’s ideals seem about as good as a developer of a single parcel can do to prove a concept and get the ball rolling. I hope they are vey successful and make lots of money to prove the concept elsewhere, which can translate into lower price points, mixed use, 15 minute cities, etc.

I recently read that book after hearing the author interviewed by both Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman. It gave me a new perspective on motivation and “happiness”, and closed the loop on these ideas as so practically described by MMM. Satisfaction, contentment, and motivation come to us by way of the “struggle” and the the effort of dealing with and facing challenging situations of all sorts – physical, emotional, and mental. Feeding our desires constantly – eating, entertainment, alcohol, drugs, shopping, etc. – only serve to make us less and less happy and more and more depressed. Eliminating our cravings and desires, while pursuing intentional hardships to keep us fit, sharp, and strong, ultimates results in a more satisfying state of mind and a fulfilling sense of wellbeing. It all comes together with the MMM philosophy of living a simple, frugal, productive, and healthy lifestyle.

While you’re in Arizona, you may want to check out Arcosanti, about half way between Phoenix and Sedona. It’s the original attempt at a prototype arcology, the 1960s urban planning model defined by Paolo Soleri and later popularized in Sim City and many science fiction novels. He focussed on combining dense urban living, environmental conservation, and place-based architecture. Arcosanti is itself beautiful, and it’s fascinating to see how the ideas that germinated there have slowly been manifesting in places like Culdesac.

I’ve been spending winters in Arizona for the last 10 years because my partner (also from Newfoundland) lives in Chandler. And literally, no joke, the first item that I have written down on my list of things to do in Arizona this coming winter is “go check out Cul De Sac”.

Maybe if I go and wander around there, I’ll spot your facial hair

I don’t know if it’s weird to say this, but I’d be up for a coffee or a bike ride or some hang time or whatever if you feel so inclined. It would definitely be the weirdest way that I’ve ever made a friend. In a good way.

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

#8742. Ilona Maher Now Looking to Take Rugby—and Girls’ Fitness—to the Next Level

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

During the 2024 Paris Olympics, USA women’s team rugby player Ilona Maher suddenly became a household name.

“I think for some people when they get famous, maybe it changes who they are and who they believe themselves to be,” Maher tells Muscle & Fitness. “I just never found that to be me.I think I’m kind of a similar person I was before the Paris Olympics.”

The bronze-medal winner posed on the cover of Sports Illustrated shortly after the games wrapped. From there, Maher went on to compete on Dancing with the Stars, launch a successful podcast, and secure major partnerships with brands like Maybelline New York, Adidas and Burn Boot Camp.

Although it seems like all eyes are on Maher, very few of her fans are watching her while she’s on the field that made her a celebrity.

“Honestly, it doesn’t frustrate me because we don’t have enough places for them to watch rugby,” Maher says. “So I would tell you to watch rugby. I could tell you there’s games on this weekend, but it’s not like you tune into one game, then I’ll keep watching that team.”

Despite the lack of eyeballs on the game, much like Caitlin Clark in the WNBA, Maher is credited for helping put the game back on the map and even boosting ticket sales.

“That’s where it’s hard for me is that there’s really not a lot of opportunities to watch the game,” Maher explains. “And when they want to watch me play—a lot of people would love to watch me play, but I play in places like South Africa and then I go to Perth. So if you want to wake up at 4 in the morning to watch me play the first two minutes of a game…”

Although Maher admits it’s a hard pill to swallow, she doesn’t let it discourage her and remains hopeful for the future of the sport.

“It’s a very tough thing in that I want to get more people in. I think more people should be in, but there we need more opportunities or need more things for [fans], games and in terms for them to be able to watch that are on home soil, too.”

The San Diego resident currently has her sights set on the 2028 L.A. summer games so all of her other projects get planned around her training for Team USA.

“We have meetings throughout the day and rehab and stretching to ramp the body up and whatnot,” explains Maher. “I have to do whatever timing my team says. I’m not an individual athlete that can build my life around my podcast. I have to build the podcast and everything else around my training life, I have to be in the gym at 8 a.m. with all the girls. It’s not worth it to miss a day of training when maybe something else will come up, because I do think I’m a team athlete through and through.”

Despite knowing her obligations to her teammates come first, Maher understands there’s a balance, especially to keep people intrigued in the sport for the upcoming olympic games.

“If my girls are grinding, I want to be out there grinding with them and not just taking the easy road,” Maher says. “But it is important for me to also focus on things like the podcasts or speaking, because that’s how I financially live the life I do.”

Maher admits she’s become so popular that she’s had to pass on some things to prioritize her love of the game.

“I have to say no to a lot of opportunities,” Maher says. “I will get invited to this cool event and I just have to pick my battles.”

Maher admits her newfound fame has created a “pretty hefty schedule,” her physical training remains her top priority. Her training schedule includes two daily on-field sessions along with a gym workout that can include speed and skills work, and up to about 20,000 steps of running. She also adds four days fo weightroom work, focusing explosive movements. The days she’s out of the gym, Maher is recovering and prepping to repeat the same schedule the following week.

The athlete says she thrives on pushing her limits in the weight room, especially with squats and bench presses.

“I like the ones where you really get to like to test yourself and see how much more you can do,” Maher says.

Despite being a professional athlete, Maher admits she still has her own personal wins in the gym.

“I do love dumb bell incline bench press,” explains Maher. “Where you do a weight and then you’re like, ‘I think I can do a little bit more weight!’ and you put a little more weight and you did and you’re like, ‘OK, I can do a little more weight. Those are the moments where I really love being in the gym”.

Off the field, Maher knows girls everywhere are looking up to her for guidance and empowerment, which is why she partnered with Burn Boot Camp to spread the message about their 45-minute high-intensity fitness classes.

“I just watched it and the energy and the way that these women came to this class, so excited to be there,” says Maher. They were high-fiving each other and they were getting stronger and it was the sort of community that I’m trying to foster and I think create, and that’s why I decided to work with this brand. Because I have so many girls who message me saying, ‘I wanna get strong. I wanna be strong like you. I just don’t know where to start and I’m intimidated by the gym.’

#8732. Science Has Zeroed in on Why Lifters Need Cardio for Heart Health

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Every gym (real gym) has a dude like this—we used to call them “fire plugs” (if you’re not from New York, that means fire hydrant). He has arms like sewer pipes, a chest like a gun safe, zero degrees of V-taper, and he’d probably be proud of the fact that he has a squat rack in his living room in case he needs some extra sets—your basic Midwestern corn-fed Jethro type. The exact guy you would never imagine seeing on a treadmill.

Cardio? That’s what people do when they don’t have huge muscles to worry about. Besides, he can see his abs (ab, actually, but it’s like a rock). What more evidence of health could anybody possibly need?

That depends on how long Jethro wants to live. A study recently published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise looked at 562,234 adults who had undergone clinical treadmill testing. Researchers wanted to know whether measuring cardiorespiratory fitness improved predictions of who would die over the following decade, beyond the usual suspects: age, sex, high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol problems, and smoking. The answer was yes. Not because the treadmill possesses magical cognitive powers, but because how much work your heart and lungs can support tells doctors something the other numbers don’t.

The researchers measured peak exercise capacity in Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET). It’s a way of expressing how much energy a physical activity demands relative to rest. In the study, the bottom fifth of fitness fell below five METs. After adjusting for traditional risk factors, the estimated ten-year mortality risk in that least-fit group was 32.9 percent, compared with 13.4 percent among the fitter participants. That’s a considerable difference, even allowing for the fact that these were people referred for clinical exercise tests, not a random cross-section of every healthy person walking around America.

Another number worth understanding correctly is that each additional MET of measured fitness was associated with a 16 percent lower hazard of death over follow-up. Notice I said associated. Not caused. The researchers did not take half a million people, put some on treadmills, leave the others on the couch, and wait ten years to see who was still kicking. This was an observational analysis. Healthier people may be able to exercise harder because they’re healthier in the first place. The study accounted for several major risk factors, but it cannot eliminate every possible explanation.

Nor did adding fitness transform mortality prediction into a crystal ball. The model’s discrimination score improved from 0.662 to 0.682 when cardiorespiratory fitness was included. That’s statistically meaningful and potentially useful, but modest. The headline isn’t that doctors can now tell you the day you’ll die by watching you jog, but rather that a basic measure of physical capacity deserves a seat at the table alongside blood pressure and the rest of the measurable health markers.

What I find fascinating is the cultural blind spot this exposes. Bodybuilders understand that muscle matters, as do strength, bone loading, glucose regulation, mobility, and the ability to get yourself up off the toilet when you’re eighty—all excellent reasons to keep lifting. Somewhere along the line, a segment of the iron community decided that cardio was bad. It was either an inconvenience or an enemy that ate muscle, or both. A lot of old-school, Arnold-era bodybuilders didn’t do cardio. Then suddenly the Life Cycle was invented, and a lot of us felt good about adding endurance training to our mix, mainly because of the massive calves and quads we started to see on Olympic cyclists. So, maybe there’s something to this? Blasphemy!

Until you consider your heart and your potential lifespan, with or without cardio and with or without muscle.

Of course, if you’re a bodybuilder, you’re going to take an extremist position. But you don’t have to become a distance runner. In fact, if your knees, hips, or general disposition object to running, there are bicycles, rowing machines, swimming pools, incline walks, and any number of ways to get your breathing up without pounding pavement. The practical target isn’t to chase a laboratory number you saw in an article. It’s to build enough aerobic capacity that ordinary life doesn’t feel like a stress test. Start where you are, progress gradually, and if you have symptoms or known heart disease, get medical guidance before going all out.

I still think a man should be strong. But if he’s strong enough to deadlift a Buick and gets gassed carrying groceries up one flight of stairs, we might have overlooked something. For the slight handful of you who compete at a very high level, doing cardio is etched into your coach’s DNA at this point. You have no choice. Except to keep doing it after the show is over. The rest of you, do cardio! Times have changed, technology has changed, and research has accumulated. Adding these data to the mountain of evidence thus collected on the topic, the overall consensus, if your desire is longevity, is simple: the lighter, stronger, leaner, and more cardiovascularly fit you are, the longer you get to bother everyone.
