Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Hawaii saver availability on United can be tight, especially during peak travel periods. Here's your playbook:

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

The math behind one of travel rewards' best-kept secrets

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

Building a company with a cofounder puts you through pressures nobody warns you about, plus the usual startup whiplash. Noah was our co-founder at Alertive Healthcare, our previous startup. He led product, engineering and design teams. He thinks like an engineer. The question he asks reframes the entire problem, and then he proceeds to build the answer.

Here’s the problem he found. Every physician in an ambulatory clinic runs against a clock, and the tell is the glancing. The wall clock. The watch. The timer in the screen’s corner. Patients catch every one of those looks, and they read them. Noah fixed it with an app, and he fixed it elegantly.

Article’s below. See whether his solution works for you. Full disclosure: Noah is a friend. I was paid no cash, no coins, no crypto and no farm eggs to write this. I just think he’s onto something.

I originally built Haptica Timer for my wife, who is a physician.

Like many clinicians, she spends much of her day moving from one patient visit to the next. She is constantly balancing two responsibilities that can sometimes feel at odds: being fully present with the patient in front of her while also staying aware of a demanding clinic schedule.

She did not want to keep looking at the wall clock. She did not want to glance at her phone or repeatedly raise her wrist during a conversation. Even when those actions are completely innocent, they can make a patient feel rushed or leave them wondering whether the physician is still listening.

What she needed was simple: a quiet way to understand how much time had passed without visibly checking the time.

That was the starting point for Haptica Timer.

The original idea was to create subtle vibration cues that could be felt on the wrist without interrupting a conversation. Just as importantly, the timer needed to repeat automatically.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

A clinician should not have to remember to start another timer before every appointment or continually manage an app throughout the day.

Instead, the timing pattern could follow the natural rhythm of the clinic schedule, repeating from one visit to the next.

The goal was never to force every patient encounter into a rigid block of time. Some appointments need more time, and physicians must always be free to respond to what the patient needs.

The goal was simply to give clinicians a private sense of where they were in the visit, reduce the need to manually track time, and help the day move more smoothly without taking attention away from the patient.

The rest of this article is written by Jorge Sanchez, one of my former co-founders at Alertive Healthcare.

A patient is explaining something important.

The appointment may have started as a routine follow-up, but another concern has surfaced. It deserves attention. At the same time, the clinician knows the visit is beginning to run long and that another patient is waiting.

This is a normal part of medicine. Patient visits do not always follow a predictable path.

The challenge goes beyond simply keeping appointments short. It is remaining engaged with the person in front of you while still respecting the time of every patient who comes afterward.

Most clinicians develop their own ways of managing this. They glance at the clock, check the computer, look down at a watch, or try to estimate how much time has passed.

None of these approaches is necessarily wrong, but they’re all rather visible.

Patients may notice when attention shifts, particularly during emotional, personal, or complicated conversations. Even a quick glance can change the feeling in the room.

At the same time, losing awareness of time can affect the rest of the clinic day. A few additional minutes across several appointments can create longer waits, less time for documentation, hurried transitions, and increasing pressure on both clinicians and staff.

The problem is not the clock itself. The problem is needing to continually look for it.

A traditional timer is designed to capture your attention.

It makes a sound, displays a notification, lights up a screen, or requires you to look at it. Those features are useful in many settings, but they are not always appropriate during a medical visit.

An audible alarm would interrupt the conversation. A phone notification could feel out of place. A visible countdown could become another thing competing for the clinician’s attention.

The better solution was a less noticeable timer.

A subtle vibration could provide awareness without changing the conversation. The clinician could feel that a certain amount of time had passed and decide what, if anything, to do with that information.

That cue might prompt the clinician to summarize the discussion, confirm the care plan, address the patient’s final concern, or decide that the conversation needs to continue.

One of the most practical parts of Haptica is its ability to run repeating timers.

Clinic schedules often follow a regular cadence. Appointments may be scheduled in 15, 20, 30, or 40-minute blocks, sometimes with a short period between visits for documentation or transition.

Once the timing pattern is configured, the timer can repeat automatically.

This means the clinician does not need to start a new timer before every patient. There is no need to repeatedly open the app or remember to reset it as the day progresses.

For example, a physician might choose to receive one gentle cue when most of the visit has passed and another near the scheduled end. The timer can then pause briefly and begin the next cycle automatically for the following appointment.

This repeating pattern is important because it allows the timer to support the workflow without becoming another workflow to manage.

The experience is less like operating a stopwatch and more like maintaining a quiet awareness of the clinic’s rhythm.

A typical appointment may include reviewing concerns, gathering relevant history, performing an examination, discussing options, answering questions, agreeing on a plan, documenting the encounter, and preparing for the next patient.

When time awareness is lost early in the visit, the final portions can become compressed. The clinician may have less time to explain the plan, complete documentation, or transition thoughtfully to the next appointment.

A discreet timing cue can help the clinician recognize where they are in that process.

It may provide an opportunity to move from information gathering into decision-making, begin summarizing the plan, or identify a concern that deserves a separate follow-up rather than trying to address everything at once.

The repeating timer also reduces the small amount of mental and operational effort involved in managing separate timers throughout the day. Once configured, it can continue through the clinic schedule with minimal interaction.

During a routine follow-up, a subtle vibration lets the physician know that most of the scheduled time has passed.

Nothing interrupts the conversation. The patient does not hear or see anything.

The physician may begin bringing the visit together by reviewing the plan, confirming the next steps, and asking whether there is one final concern that needs to be addressed.

The cue does not end the visit. It helps the physician recognize that it may be time to transition naturally toward a conclusion.

During another visit, the vibration occurs while a patient is discussing something emotional or unexpected.

The physician feels the cue but chooses not to act on it.

The conversation continues because the patient needs more time.

This is an important part of how Haptica is intended to work. It provides awareness, and leaves the clinician to decide what the moment requires.

On a busy day, small delays can build quickly.

A few extra minutes across several morning appointments may become a significant delay by the afternoon. Patients wait longer, staff members work to catch up, documentation may accumulate, and the clinician may begin to feel increasingly rushed.

A repeating timer does not solve every scheduling or workflow challenge.

It can, however, provide a consistent sense of time throughout the day without requiring the clinician to repeatedly manage it.

That awareness may help identify when a visit is drifting, when it is time to begin summarizing, or when a concern may be better addressed through a separate follow-up.

Even when the physician decides to continue the visit, that decision is made with a clearer understanding of where the day stands.

Being present does not require completely losing awareness of time. In some cases, greater time awareness may make it easier to remain present.

When clinicians know where they are in a visit, they may feel less pressure to mentally track the clock. They can focus more fully on the patient and make a deliberate decision about whether to continue, transition, or arrange additional time.

The timer stays in the background. Clinical judgment remains at the center.

We did not want to create another complicated productivity system.

Clinicians already work with numerous systems, alerts, documentation requirements, and administrative tasks. Haptica was designed to address one specific problem without adding another layer of complexity.

#8699. The Ultimate Life Coach

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

To most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

So I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:

I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

See, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:

I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

It’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

As part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and issues, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:

I now realize that things are more like this:

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

So the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

For me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

While the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

Thank you for this post, MMM. Currently struggling with similar situations in life and I hope to put this to good use.

Started reading your blog in 2018 and it has been a constant source of inspiration and help. I am 32 and left the relatively high paying banking job at 27 to build a start up. Ultimately the businesses haven’t been financially successful over the last 5 years but your wisdom ensured I kept my expenses low enough (even while living in London) that I haven’t felt the need to rush back to get a stable salary.

In fact, my girlfriend and I have done the opposite. We converted a van ourselves and are travelling around Europe in it. Naturally our expenses fell even further.

Despite being ‘only’ 32 and not financially free in the absolute sense (i.e. 25x spend invested), we have enough invested and our need to spend is so low that I feel a lot of what you have described above. I have spent the last 3 months frustrated with my lack of productivity and took the wussy approach of thinking ‘ah I have just been too lucky, I have the big safety net of a great family and an education. And my needs are so low that I don’t have the desire to make loads of money therefore I don’t have the motivation to do the work’.

This, of course, is rubbish. I know deep down we want to be creative, productive and a service to others but it has just been tricky finding the ‘why’ to do it. Your article here will be a great help. It is incredible how timely your articles seem to be in my own life.

Only this week I seem to have overcome the first hurdle a little and have started writing my own newsletter. An interesting stat that I read recently that has really helped with my motivation was this. People that do ‘hard’ things for long-term reasons, i.e. ‘I exercise to live longer’ or ‘I exercise to be healthy’, do 30% less exercise than people who exercise for the immediate benefits like ‘I want to feel better today!’ or ‘I exercise to feel more energised TODAY’.

I gave this reframing a go for sitting down to write. I changed from ‘I want to write so that in the future I will have a newsletter that serves others and makes me money’ to ‘I want to write because of the state of flow I will feel in the moment and the sense of achievement I will feel TODAY’. It has completely energised me and increased my motivation to do the thing I have been putting off because ‘I don’t have to do it’.

I will implement your advice above alongside this reframing and hopefully soon you will be reading my newsletter in the same way I have read yours over the years :).

Nice to hear Elliot! And thanks for sharing.

It’s interesting how the money game can be motivating for many of us, to the point where it “fools” us into doing things that are great for other reasons. Strangely, my own son has the opposite wiring: despite the fact that we have kept his upbringing pretty simple and avoided “rich kid syndrome”, making sure he earns and pays for the material possessions he wants himself, he still doesn’t have the same drive to earn and accumulate Green Employees that I had. Yet he’s still SUPER motivated to work on his own stuff regardless.

This is just the motivation I need right now. I stopped working over two years ago and can relate to it feeling like a double-edged sword.

Some things that make me feel healthy, happy, and strong that I know I should do more of: weight training, mountain biking, backpacking in the mountains, keeping my house and garage workshop clean and organized, designing and building things, helping other people with home projects, cooking.

One thing I do that helps me stay focused on these things is turn off ALL notifications on my phone, then selectively turn on the few notifications I actually want to know about. I only get notified for text messages, voice mails, calendar reminders, and a few other things. There are often days when I get zero notifications on my phone.

This may not be for everyone, but I also don’t use any social media or read/watch hardly any news. I do watch youtube, but no facebook, instagram, twitter, tik tok, etc. For me all of these things feel like they are vying to “steal” my focus and make it harder to have a calm mind and energy to focus on the things I know I should be doing. I highly recommend people at least try this for a while and see if they feel different. You can always add things back in that you actually do miss. I think MMM wrote an article about this “low information diet” a while ago.

I think what you are recommending is good advice for everyone: ALL phone notifications off except for direct texts/calls from your closest friends and loved ones.

And, no social media apps should even be installed on anyone’s phones. You should have to sit down and open up your olde fashioned laptop or desktop computer to get access to this info, and it shouldn’t happen more than once a day after your walk/run and your work and your lifting is done.

Funny story: Instagram has a deliberately crippled user interface so that you have to use their phone app to post videos and do certain other things. I don’t have a personal instagram account, but I do like to share some MMM stuff occasionally because it helps me find new readers for the website/newsletter. So every time I want to post something of that type, I have to re-install the app, post it, and then delete the app again.

A person with more willpower than I would be able to just leave it on his phone and simply never open it. But I find that just like having a cheesecake in my fridge, if it’s there I will start indulging. So I avoid the temptation by just not having it available.

I’d get a spare phone for that situation, kept in a locked drawer if necessary.

Perhaps you are already aware that this little exercise . . .

I want to work out today. I don’t feel like it. ^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^ I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

. . . is pure Stoicism, a topic you have touched on before.

That little voice in your head that says “I don’t feel like it” is what the Stoics called “an impression.” You have clearly learned to apply “prosoche” (mindfulness would be a good translation of this Greek word) to interrogate that impression. Then you applied natural wisdom (one of the Stoic virtues) to reach the logical conclusion that surrendering to that impression would not be in your best interest.

There is another Stoic echo in your rediscovered commitment to exercise. The Stoics strongly believed that it was crucial to constantly test oneself, whether that meant fasting, walking barefoot in the now, or undertaking difficult or unpleasant tasks.

So well done! You are proving an apt “prokopton” (one who is making progress to becoming a Stoic sage).

As a retired person I can really relate to this. For me it’s not the lack of desire to do hard things, it’s the easy distracting nature of the phone. I get bored, pull out my phone, then wonder where the last eight hours went.

People with jobs and young kids have to put down the phone to go to work, or take the kids to school. I could spend 100% of my time on YouTube, and my brain will do that if I let it.

My retired quality of life improved immensely when I started keeping my phone and computer in my office out of reach.

Now I get bored, feel uncomfortable, then go and do something. That feeling of boredom and discomfort is critical to making me do the things that actually bring joy to my life.

Boredom is a signal that I have spare energy that should be used for something. Phones alleviate boredom and kill motivation

Hey RH, thanks for following along with that. Throughout my stay there, I kept this page updated, and it’s now in its final form with all my thoughts so far: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Summary: there is *some* community forming there, but not as much as I expected going in – they’re still working on building out the neighborhood so it’s a tough chicken-and-egg problem to crack. How do you attract people who really want to hang out with their neighbors rather than just people looking to hide away in their apartments? The Culdesac team are fantastic however, and of course the physical architecture of the place is beautiful. So I think they are doing the right things to build it out.

Glad to hear you’re picking up Extreme Ownership! As someone who is still in his working years, it’s made the way I think about getting work done much better. In software engineering, sometimes shit just goes wrong. Knowing that almost everything can be avoided by us engineers doing a better and robust job has improved the way I work and has made me _less_ stressed, because the work I do is better and more well thought out from the start. Even when something does go wrong, it’s just a learning experience that allows me to avoid those pitfalls in the future.

This book is even better for your social relationships though! Most of the time, you can be the ignition to a better relationship with someone. I’ve seen it many times where relationships you want drift away because neither side initiates social interaction enough with the other. “If they really care, they’d reach out.” Turns out, if you take ownership and reach out, you’ll see them a lot more and be happier as a result. The same thing applies for someone toxic in your life. Tired of this person bringing you down? Take ownership and remove yourself from the equation. (Obviously there are circumstances where this doesn’t apply, but you’ll know it when you see it).

Plus the narration of the audiobook is just great. Jocko has that Seal Team motivational way of speaking that makes you get your shit together!

I was in a similar situation. Thank you for writing this post. I thought everyone else had their act together, so hearing that you had similar challenges made me feel ‘normal’. I also discovered Goggins, and have been using it to do things I know I need to do, but procrastinated on

I have noticed a lot less posts over the past year.. Is this part of of “not doing” what you want to do.. or something else?

Try a HappyLight by Verilux or similar product. Helped me a lot, especially in the winter months.

Thank you for posting this and articulating ideas many are feeling on this blog. I’ve been facing much of this same internal dialog from the perspective of working 20 years at a career I enjoy that pays well. With that job I enjoy I still think about quality of life and wonder about meaning as my children grow older and my spouse and I get closer to financial freedom.

It’s a weird place to be to doubt internally whether I actually want to retire as the feasibility becomes more real. Anyone else feeling the same and concerned not putting myself in the situation explained in the blog is actually easier than having to deal with the procrastination?

Secondly, a coworker in a similar situation volunteers for local search and rescue. It gives him a bigger picture reason to stay in great shape. It’s got me thinking about doing the same as I approach my late 40’s.

I have found a social approach works best for keeping me motivated to work out. My partner is training for a canoe trip in Canada, so we both ride our bikes to the gym twice a week. On both days I go to a weight training class for older adults. I like the work out, the instructors and my classmates. Oh yeah, and they play Beatles music.

I also get yearly DXA scans. Last year my scans were horrible and that motivated me to start regular strength training. This year I have improved and that motivates me to keep working out.

Not everything is mental unfortunately. I have all kinds of motivation and willingness to push myself, but no matter what I do, my body is just not in the condition that it was 10 – 15 years ago, and the aches and pains that result from pushing myself prevent me from doing anything more than walking at this point in my life. So, this advice is great if you don’t have any medical conditions preventing you from pushing yourself, however, I believe that there are many people out there like myself who are not built like Goggins.

I realise you have said you don’t swallow the whole Goggins creed, Mr. Moustache, but Goggins? In any measure? Really?

I am surprised you haven’t learnt by now that always pushing your limits, redlining your body, is not a formula for health, fitness and well-being; it is the road to injury and burnout.

There are countless examples of exercise fanatics who started off thinking, with Nietzsche, that ‘That which doesn’t kill me makes me stronger’. They end up realising that ‘That which doesn’t kill me can still cripple me’.

Just look at poor old Ronnie Coleman. https://youtu.be/kq0Sm4kAp4Y?si=_ma2zjT_WoWVi4wC

But after many injuries, all self-inflicted and therefore avoidable, I have developed a different philosophy: Progress over perfection; You won’t improve from something you can’t recover from; Little by little, step by step, work on your weaknesses and limitations; No brain, no gain.

Could your procrastination stem from thinking that exercise is a gruelling, penitential task? Why not just resolve to show up everyday and just do something — some mobility work, an easy jog, a few sets of easy pull-ups and hanging leg raises? Some days that will put you in the mood to push harder, go further— fine. Other days you can stop there — also fine. Just keep showing up and making deposits into the Bank (or ETF, or whatever) of Fitness. They will add up, and sometimes compound, just like money. Health and fitness is a long game, just like saving and investment.

There is definitely a time and place to test your mettle — generally in a competition or emergency. But suffering is not how you get fitter. ‘The ability to suffer during a workout is just one skill. Don’t over-focus on it. You also need to train a hundred other skills’.https://youtu.be/0h23IANIg6Q For most workouts, the goal should be to finish feeling better than when you started. Energised, not exhausted. If tired, sore, and injured are the side-effects, is it worth it?

Of course, who am I to say what will motivate you? But I know that when I changed my outlook from struggle-&-suffer to small, manageable steps, every day my hesitation vanished and I became keen to show up.

#8696. Nearly 150 Doctors Walked Off the Job at a Hospital With $6 Billion In Revenue

According to the 2026 Medscape Physician Compensation Report, average physician pay reached $386,000 this year, up 3% from 2025 and enough to outpace the 2.7% core inflation rate.

Eight specialties crossed half a million dollars, led by orthopedic surgery at $611,000. 53% of physicians said they feel fairly compensated individually, the highest share in years. All wonderful news.

However, 61% of physicians still believe the profession as a whole is underpaid, and the average workweek barely budged. 63% of physicians blame bureaucratic work and electronic health records for their burnout. 14% of physicians say that they’re planning to leave clinical medicine altogether because of it.

And hospital systems aren’t going out of their way to ease the situation. Private equity and mergers bring in money that should help expand staff and provide a better work environment.

On the contrary, doctors face heavier workloads than ever with no room for PTO. All to protect the bottom line for those at the top.

Private health systems chasing profit and the policy turmoil of declining reimbursement and Medicaid funding work together to create the perfect storm of doctors at their wits’ end. This month we saw exactly how that plays out in real life.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities hospitals went on strike, in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.

This was not a spur-of-the-moment decision, but came after three years of bargaining that went nowhere. The health system had made $6 billion in 2025 revenue but was negotiating pay and sick time as if there were nothing left to give.

The cherry on top? A $26 billion merger behind closed doors.

In case you missed it: The Great Debate of Physician Unionization

Doctors represented by Doctors Council SEIU picketed outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and its Unity campus in Fridley for four days starting September 14, carrying signs reading “patients over profits.”

The union voted to unionize in 2023, sat through more than 60 bargaining sessions and authorized the strike with 90% support in July before giving the required 10 days’ notice.

Allina downplayed the disruption, stating that the union represents only about 10% of the physicians credentialed at both campuses and told the Minnesota Reformer that 37 union doctors crossed the picket line while 40 weren’t scheduled to work that week. Both campuses stayed open. The strike ran alongside a separate seven-day walkout by roughly 60 Allina hospice nurses.

Hospitalist Dr. Amber Galarowicz, on the union’s bargaining team, said that the fight isn’t just about pay. “We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” she said.

Paid sick leave was likely the biggest factor. Minnesota law entitles full-time workers to six days a year but the doctors say they can’t take paid time off when they’re sick without dipping into vacation days.

Allina says its physicians already have paid leave and that it’s in compliance with state law. Never mind the fact that healthcare workers face a higher risk of getting ill.

“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” said Dr. Alia Sharif, another bargaining team hospitalist.

Dr. John Wurst, who was part of the strike, said that doctors are also fighting to keep decision-making in physician hands, pointing to artificial intelligence tools that now weigh in on insurance billing as one example of ground already lost.

“We feel like we’re being excluded from decisions that affect the care of our patients,” Wurst said, adding that leaving physicians out of those calls means medical resources won’t end up allocated in a way that actually serves the community.

Cost of living adjustments have been part of the back and forth since last fall. This is amid rising inflation and fuel costs.

Coverage itself is also disputed. Because doctors often work across multiple Allina facilities, the two sides can’t agree on which physicians the union contract actually covers.

Doctors need to spend at least 20% of their time at Unity or Mercy to qualify for the bargaining unit but how that 20% gets calculated is still up in the air.

Apart from this local dispute, doctors across the nation are contending with policy changes that directly affects how much they earn.

Medicare’s 2026 physician fee schedule finalized a 2.5% “efficiency adjustment” that CMS says reflects services becoming easier to perform over time.

The policy applies to roughly 7,700 billing codes, including surgical procedures, diagnostic imaging interpretation, outpatient interventions, interventional pain management and orthopedic services.

Learn more: A Physician’s Guide to Medicare’s Specialty Care Changes — What’s Really Happening?

By law, Medicare physician payments have to stay budget neutral, meaning a raise for one group of doctors requires a cut somewhere else. Primary care physicians and time-based services keep the 2.5% increase Congress passed last year.

Specialists performing procedures have to watch that same increase get wiped out by the efficiency adjustment, and in some cases end up with a net cut once other changes are factored in.

The American Medical Association says that these changes will affect certain specialties more than others. More than a third of oncologists face cuts as steep as 20%. Over half of internists can expect reductions of 5% or more, and the same goes for 80% of infectious disease physicians.

One physician commented that as one of two infectious disease specialists in her region, the cuts would force her to refuse care to Medicare and Medicaid patients or simply retire.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 reconciliation law will cut federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years, and 16 million people are projected to lose coverage through Medicaid or the ACA marketplace.

The layoffs stemming from these policy changes are no longer hypothetical. Back in June, Hennepin Healthcare in Minneapolis, in the same metro area as Allina’s Mercy and Unity campuses, announced roughly 100 layoffs this year and cut 100 inpatient beds, citing a $50 million shortfall tied directly to Medicaid revenue losses.

Trinity Health said it expects to lose $1.5 billion to “recent and future government policy changes.” Baptist Health in Arkansas laid off 150 employees, including 10 physicians, while shutting down its nephrology, pulmonary, oncology and infectious disease services.

Allina itself is telling employees that its economic decisions stem from “rising costs for drugs, supplies and labor, ongoing reimbursement pressures, increases in claim denials from insurance companies, and anticipated impacts from federal policy and reimbursement changes.”

Also read: What Physicians Should Know About the CMS Cut That Shaves Your Same-Day E/M Payment in Half

On top of all this is Allina’s proposed merger with Sutter Health, a California nonprofit, that would combine the two systems into a $26 billion operation spanning 39 hospitals across three states.

The merger is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office and opposed by labor unions who warn that consolidation tends to raise costs for patients while suppressing wage growth for the workers providing care.

Sharif said she doesn’t expect the union to block the deal but she’d like a community benefits agreement that shields against layoffs and service cuts, similar to one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health over its acquisition of a Robbinsdale hospital.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

For those who aren’t working at Mercy or Unity, this may feel abstract. It’s not.

Physician unionization has been on the rise because things that used to work, like individual negotiation, specialty societies lobbying CMS, and professional goodwill, keep losing to system-level budget decisions.

If you’re an employed physician, this deserves your attention. The same reimbursement structure and Medicaid cuts may come for whatever health system signs your paycheck.

Strikes make headlines because everyone has an opinion on them. Bureaucrats like to dismiss legitimate physician demands as unreasonable. But the jig is up, and the people are decrying the monopolization of our healthcare system.

The question is, what will it take to stop the consolidation machine?

#8694. Three Months Into Expert Witness Work, I Get the Appeal

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality shows up in distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.

When you’re ambitious, your mind keeps moving the finish line. Even when things are going well, you still hear the same thought: I should be doing more. You don’t always have the same energy.

A big context-dependent factor of your lifestyle is how, where, and when you spend money, and this can be influenced by whether or not you’re receiving a regularly scheduled paycheck. Studies show retirees are often overly frugal with their savings.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Avios are accessible from virtually every major transferable points currency:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Go to ba.com, log into your Executive Club account, and complete the award booking. Enter passenger details, select seats, and confirm.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book.
